To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the egc gene locus encoding the novel superantigens seg, sei, sen and seo and the SaPIboV-encoded sec and tst genes are predominant among S. aureus isolates obtained from cows, goats and sheep, but not among isolates from rabbits, chickens and a cat.
novel staphylococcus enterotoxins predominate in Staphylococci from animals and that further uncharacterised superantigens are present in bovine Staphylococcu isolates.
novel superantigen genes predominate among Staphyloccus aureus isolates in animals and that further uncharacterised superantigens may be present in some isolates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular epidemiology of staphylococcus enterotoxins, which are superantigens, and their role in animal disease and zoonosis.
the identification of the most important SAg genes in animal isolates of S. aureus.
the molecular epidemiology of S. aureus in animal reservoirs, which is of interest for the development of strategies to reduce the transmission of S. aureu s to humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the egc cluster of SAg genes is a major virulence factor for staphylococcus in animals, and that the egc genes are more important in the pathogenesis of S. aureus infections of ruminants than of bovines.
the egc cluster genes are most frequent in bovine isolations, while the sec-tst combination is most prevalent among ovine or caprine strains.
S. aureus isolates of animal origin carry SAg genes at frequencies that are different from human isolates, but are also similar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the S. aureus isolates of the present study are more likely to be pathogenic to humans, as they are more likely to possess the sec and tst gene combination than to possess the egc cluster.
the egc cluster is predominant in S. aureuses from animals, while the SaPIbovirulent island and the tst gene are more prevalent in human isolates.

the most common combination of superantigen genes is the egc cluster in 47 isolations, the sec, tst, and sel combination in 44 isolations, the egc gene complex lacking seg in 11 isolations, and the sec, tst genes without sel in seven isolations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the egc cluster is the predominant source of SAg genes in S. aureu s isolates from animals.
the S. aureus strains isolated from animals are a rich source of new superantigens.
the SAg gene profiles of S. aureus strains isolated from different animal hosts are different.
